etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English reden, from Old English rǣdan (“to counsel, advise, consult; interpret, read”), from Proto-West Germanic *rādan, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną (“advise, counsel”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₁dʰ- (“to arrange”).

Cognate with Scots rede, red (“to advise, counsel, decipher, read”), Saterland Frisian räide (“to advise, counsel”), West Frisian riede (“to advise, counsel”), Dutch raden (“to advise; guess”), German raten (“to advise; guess”), Danish råde (“to advise”), Swedish råda (“to advise, counsel”), Persian رده (rade, “to order, to arrange, class”). In West Germanic the verb had a sense “interpret”, which developed further into “interpret letters” in English and “interpret by intuition, guess” on the continent. Compare rede.

definitions.definition: (transitive or intransitive) To look at and interpret letters or other information that is written.

quote.citation: 1661, John Fell, The Life of the most learned, reverend and pious Dr. H. Hammond‎[2]:
quote.text: During the whole time of his abode in the university he generally spent thirteen hours of the day in study; by which assiduity besides an exact dispatch of the whole course of philosophy, he read over in a manner all classic authors that are extant […]

quote.citation: 1982, Robert M. Evenson, “"Liberated" Woman"”, in The Cincinnati Enquirer:
quote.text: She reads Playgirl magazine, goes to a male-strip joint and then complains about sexual harassment on the job.

quote.citation: 1983, James C. H. Shen, “A Round of Calls”, in Robert Myers, editor, The U.S. & Free China: How the U.S. Sold Out Its Ally‎[3], Washington, D.C.: Acropolis Books Ltd., →ISBN, page 112:
quote.text: On this occasion he was carrying in his right hand a copy of the English-language China News, an odd touch because the President did not read English.

definitions.definition: (transitive or intransitive) To speak aloud words or other information that is written. (often construed with a to phrase or an indirect object)

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: In the old days, to my commonplace and unobserving mind, he gave no evidences of genius whatsoever. He never read me any of his manuscripts,  […]  and therefore my lack of detection of his promise may in some degree be pardoned.

quote.citation: 1921, Ben Travers, chapter 1, in A Cuckoo in the Nest, Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page & Company, published 1925, →OCLC:
quote.text: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To read work(s) written by (a named author).
(transitive) To interpret, or infer a meaning, significance, thought, intention, etc., from.
To consist of certain text.
(ergative) Of text, etc., to be interpreted or read in a particular way.
(transitive, often humorous) To substitute (a corrected piece of text in place of an erroneous one); used to introduce an emendation of a text.

quote.citation: 1832, John Lemprière et al., Bibliotheca classica, Seventh Edition, W. E. Dean, page 263:
quote.text: In Livy, it is nearly certain that for Pylleon we should read Pteleon, as this place is mentioned in connection with Antron.

quote.citation: 2023 May 12, Lia Mappoura, “I tried Glossier's brand new G Suit lip crèmes so you don't have to – you're welcome”, in Cosmopolitan‎[4]:
quote.text: I also did a long-wear test, as y'do and after scoffing my face with some food (read: I am feral when it comes to a midday snack, so what), the striking colour that I was wearing, named 'Jet', had stayed put. Pigment, check ✅.

definitions.definition: (informal, usually ironic) Used after a euphemism to introduce the intended, more blunt meaning of a term.

quote.citation: 2009, Suzee Vlk et al., The GRE Test for Dummies, 6th edition, Wiley Publishing, →ISBN, page 191:
quote.text: Eliminate illogical (read: stupid) answer choices.

definitions.definition: (transitive, telecommunications) To be able to hear what another person is saying over a radio connection.

quote.citation: 1968, Stanley Kubrick, Arthur C. Clarke, 2001: A Space Odyssey, spoken by Dave Bowman (Keir Dullea):
quote.text: Hello, HAL. Do you read me, HAL?

definitions.definition: (transitive, rail transport) To observe and comprehend (a displayed signal).
(transitive, Commonwealth, except Scotland) To study (a subject) at a high level, especially at university.

quote.citation: 1956, Anthony Burgess, Time for a Tiger (The Malayan Trilogy), published 1972, page 94:
quote.text: Crabbe wanted him to go to England, to read for a degree there.

definitions.definition: (computing, transitive) To fetch data from (a storage medium, etc.).
(transitive, LGBTQ) To recognise (someone) as being transgender.
(at first especially in the black LGBTQ community) To call attention to the flaws of (someone) in either a playful, a taunting, or an insulting way.

quote.citation: 1976 August 7, Tommi Avicolli, “The Politics of Camp”, in Gay Community News, page 9:
quote.text: I've seen drags "read" an unattractive transsexual until she was almost in tears.

quote.citation: 1997, Framing Culture: Africanism, Sexuality and Performance, page 186 (also discussing Paris is Burning):
quote.text: Snapping, we are told, comes from reading, or exposing hidden flaws in a person's life, and out of reading comes shade  […]

quote.citation: 2003, Philip Auslander, Performance: Media and technology, page 179:
quote.text: CB [a black gay person being quoted]: "So, one time I read him and we were standing downstairs at the front desk in the dorm and I read him and there was this little bell  […] ." In the first example, the interviewee [CB] used snapping to read his white friend in a playful way,  […] .

quote.citation: 2013, Queer Looks, page 114 (discussing Paris is Burning and "the ball world"):
quote.text: [One] assumes that such language contests are racially motivated—black folks talking back to white folks. However, the ball world makes it clear that blacks can read each other too.

definitions.definition: (go) To imagine sequences of potential moves and responses without actually placing stones.
(obsolete) To think, believe; to consider (that).

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: But now, faire Ladie, comfort to you make, / And read […]  / That short reuenge the man may ouertake  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To advise; to counsel. See rede.

quote.citation: 1528 October 12 (Gregorian calendar), William Tyndale, “The .IIIJ. Senses of yͤ Scripture”, in The Obediẽce of a Christen Man […], [Antwerp]: [Johannes Hoochstraten], →OCLC, folio cxlvi, verso:
quote.text: [T]herfore / I red the [thee] / gete the [thee] to Gods vvorde ãd [and] therby trye all doctrine and agenſt that receave nothinge.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 6:
quote.text: This is the wandring wood, this Errours den, / A monster vile, whom God and man does hate: / Therefore I read beware.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To tell; to declare; to recite.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: But read how art thou named, and of what kin.

definitions.definition: A reading or an act of reading, especially of an actor's part of a play or a piece of stored data.

quote.citation: 1879, Frederick James Furnivall, letter to the editor of "The Spectator":
quote.text: One newswoman here lets magazines for a penny a read.

quote.citation: 1958, Philip Larkin, Self's the Man:
quote.text: And when he finishes supper / Planning to have a read at the evening paper / It's Put a screw in this wall— / He has no time at all […]

quote.citation: 2006, MySQL administrator's guide and language reference, page 393:
quote.text: In other words, the system can do 1200 reads per second with no writes, the average write is twice as slow as the average read, and the relationship is linear.

definitions.definition: (in combination) Something to be read; a written work.
A person's interpretation or impression of something.
(at first especially in the black LGBTQ community) An instance of reading (“calling attention to someone's flaws; a taunt or insult”).

quote.citation: 1997, Framing Culture: Africanism, Sexuality and Performance, page 186 (also discussing Paris is Burning):
quote.text: [As] Corey points out, "if you and I are both black queens then we can't call each other black queens because that's not a read. That's a [fact]."

quote.citation: 2003, Philip Auslander, Performance: Media and technology, page 185:
quote.text: Like most African-American women, Pearlie Mae uses snapping in many of the same ways that black gay men use it: to accentuate a read.

quote.citation: 2013, bell hooks, Teaching Critical Thinking: Practical Wisdom, →ISBN:
quote.text: I learned that it was acceptable to be witty, especially if you were one of the wearblackallthetime, deconstructivist, radical, feministbitchydiva girls who could give a harsh read (i.e., critique) or throw shade  […] .

definitions.definition: (biochemistry) The identification of a specific sequence of genes in a genome or bases in a nucleic acid string
